cues.text: An Orphan's Early Grief
Born on 21 March 1474 at Desenzano on the shore of Lake Garda in Lombardy, Angela Merici was orphaned at only ten years old.

She went with her elder sister to live with an uncle in the neighboring town of Salò, where they led a quiet, devout life together, reading and praying under their uncle's watchful and pious guidance.
When her sister died suddenly, without the opportunity to receive the last sacraments, Angela was thrown into grief compounded by anxious uncertainty over her sister's eternal fate.
She spent years afterward increasing her own prayers and penances on her sister's behalf, becoming a lay tertiary of the Franciscan order in her search for consolation.
Blindness on Pilgrimage
In 1524, while undertaking a pilgrimage to the Holy Land, Angela was suddenly struck blind on the island of Crete.
She chose to bear this devastating affliction rather than abandon her pilgrimage, continuing to visit Jerusalem’s sacred sites in her blindness.
On the return journey, Angela prayed before a crucifix at the very spot on Crete where the blindness had first struck her.
Her sight was restored, an event her contemporaries and later biographers alike regarded as a genuine and significant sign of divine favor.
A Reputation That Reached Rome
Angela's growing reputation for holiness and skillful religious instruction of young women eventually reached Rome itself.
During the jubilee year of 1525, Pope Clement VII, having heard of her remarkable gifts as a teacher, invited her to remain in Rome.

Angela, characteristically shunning public honor, declined the prestigious offer, choosing instead to return to the quieter work she had already begun in Brescia among girls whose families could offer them no other form of education.
Seventeen Years of Patient Preparation
Angela had received, as early as 1506, a vision she understood as a call to found a society of consecrated virgins at Brescia.
Yet she spent seventeen further years directing a loose, informal company of devout young women.
They lived not in a convent but within their own family households, meeting periodically for prayer and instruction, before finally judging the moment right to establish a formal community.

This patient, decades-long preparation reflects a hallmark of Angela's own spiritual wisdom: a conviction that genuine religious foundations should not be rushed into premature institutional form, but allowed to mature slowly under careful, prayerful guidance.
The First Teaching Order of Women
On 25 November 1535, Angela finally gathered twelve women together in a small house near the church of St. Afra in Brescia.
This founded what became known as the Company of St. Ursula — later, the Ursulines — the Church's first religious order of women dedicated specifically to educating young girls.
It was a genuinely pioneering venture in an era when formal education for girls, particularly outside wealthy families, remained rare.
Legacy
Angela died at Brescia on 27 January 1540, having led the Company for only about three years as its superior she had spent nearly two decades patiently preparing to found.
Before her death, she reportedly reassured her anxious sisters that she would remain more truly alive and more able to help them after it than she had ever been in life.
Canonized in 1807, Angela Merici remains the founding mother of Catholic women's education worldwide.
The Ursulines she established spread rapidly across Europe and later the Americas.
The Ursuline tradition became an important influence on the later development of Catholic girls' education in Europe and the Americas.
Her own insistence on flexibility, that her Rule should be adapted by her successors to the changing needs of each new age, remains an unusually forward-looking legacy for a foundress of her century.
